fascia-soffit.hubIntro: Fascia and soffit boards are the horizontal timber (or nowadays uPVC) trim running along the edge of the roof. The fascia is the vertical board you see from the street, the soffit is the underside that closes the gap between the wall and the fascia. Once these rot, water starts getting into the eaves and the rafters — replacing them is almost always cheaper than dealing with the roof damage that follows.
hubBody: The overwhelming majority of UK homeowners now go with uPVC over timber - it doesn't need painting, doesn't rot, and comes in colours (Anthracite Grey and Black Ash have overtaken white as the most-requested finish since 2020). Standard boards are 300mm deep for fascia and 150-450mm wide for soffit depending on the eaves overhang. Foil-wrapped uPVC gives a wood-grain effect if the property is period or in a conservation area.

A quality install includes over-fascia vents (a continuous slot the birds and bats can't get through) plus soffit ventilation - modern lofts need the airflow to prevent condensation. Ask specifically about ventilation on the quote, cheaper jobs often skip it and you find out two winters later when the loft insulation gets damp. Guarantee lengths vary wildly: 10 years is standard, some brands (Freefoam, Swish) will underwrite 25-year colour retention.
hubTips: Ask whether the existing timber is being fully replaced or only capped over - capping is cheaper but hides ongoing rot underneath.
Check the quote includes over-fascia venting and soffit vents to Building Regs Part F airflow standards.
Insist on aluminium nails or stainless-steel screws for fixings - galvanised nails rust and stain the boards within 5 years.
For gables above bay windows, the corner trims and joins need proper mitred corners rather than plastic corner caps - looks much better and lasts.
fascia-soffit.commonSpecs: 300mm x 18mm foil-wrapped uPVC fascia, 9mm hollow uPVC soffit board 150-450mm wide, over-fascia continuous vent, square soffit vents 25/1000mm, aluminium eaves protection tray, stainless steel fixings, colour options: white, Anthracite Grey, Black Ash, Rosewood or Golden Oak woodgrain.

guttering.hubIntro: Rainwater guttering has gone from a boring plumbing job to a proper style choice - which is why so many UK homeowners now replace working guttering just to switch from white to black or Anthracite Grey to match new windows. But guttering also does real structural work: 200 litres a minute in a heavy storm has to go somewhere, and if the fall is wrong or a joint fails you get wet walls and eventually damp inside.
hubBody: The two big variables are profile and material. Profile - Half Round, Ogee (K-style, more decorative), Deepflow (higher capacity for larger roofs). Material - uPVC is the mainstream default, cast aluminium is more expensive but looks period and doesn't sag, cast iron is authentic for pre-1930 properties but needs painting. For a standard semi, expect around 15-20 metres of gutter, 8-12 metres of downpipe, plus outlets, angles and unions.

The install matters more than the material. Correct fall (a slope of around 1:600 to 1:350 toward the outlet), brackets every 900mm minimum (600mm in exposed locations or with cast aluminium), unions with proper EPDM seals not silicone. A good installer will also check the swan-neck offset around the eaves and make sure the outlet doesn't sit right above the neighbour's driveway.
hubTips: Ask what fall the installer will set the gutter to - if they don't have a number they don't know what they're doing.
Check the quote covers new brackets, not reusing the old ones - old brackets are why the new gutter sags in year 2.
For cast aluminium, insist on stainless steel fixings and marine-grade sealant if you're within 10 miles of the coast.
Downpipes should discharge into a gulley or soakaway, not straight onto the ground - that's a Building Regs point that gets missed.
guttering.commonSpecs: Half Round or Ogee uPVC gutter 112mm, downpipe 68mm round, brackets 900mm centres, mitred external angles, running outlet, swan-neck offset, EPDM seal unions, clip-on stop ends, black / white / Anthracite Grey / Brown.

roof-replacement.hubIntro: A full roof replacement means stripping the existing covering back to the rafters, checking the timbers, laying new breathable felt and battens, and re-tiling with new concrete tiles, clay tiles or natural slates. If your roof is over 40 years old, has multiple leaks in different spots, or the timber battens have rotted, replacement is usually cheaper long-term than patching year after year. Expect it to take 3-7 working days for an average UK semi.
hubBody: The material choice drives the biggest slice of the price. Concrete interlocking tiles are the workhorse (around £45-£75 per m² fitted), clay plain tiles look far better on period property but cost more (£75-£130 per m²), and natural Welsh or Spanish slate is the top end (£120-£200 per m² and up). Underneath, the two hidden but critical items are breathable Type 1F felt (skip cheap non-breathable felt - it causes condensation in modern lofts) and pressure-treated battens graded to BS 5534.

A proper quote itemises everything: strip cost, waste disposal (skips), scaffold hire (typically 2-3 weeks), tiles and materials, new lead flashings to chimneys and abutments, new ridge system (dry-fix is now standard), new eaves and verge protection, and finally re-plastering any internal water damage. If a quote is one lump sum with no breakdown, you can't compare it fairly - always ask for the itemised version.
hubTips: Insist on dry-fix ridge and dry-fix verge as standard - mortar-bedded ridges fail within 15 years and cost as much as a repair job to redo.
Get the loft insulation topped up while the roof is off - the roofer can lay it from above without pulling up ceilings, cheapest window to do it.
Check the quote includes new lead flashings to any chimney, abutment or dormer - reusing old flashings is the #1 source of post-replacement leaks.
Ask about the warranty: manufacturer-backed guarantees (Marley, Redland, BMI) plus installer workmanship guarantees are worth 10x an installer-only guarantee.
roof-replacement.commonSpecs: Full strip and re-cover, breathable Type 1F underlay, pressure-treated BS 5534 battens 25x50mm, new interlocking concrete or clay plain tiles, dry-fix ridge with continuous vent, dry-fix verge, new lead flashings Code 4/5, mortar bedding to abutments only, scaffold and waste disposal included.

roof-repair.hubIntro: Roof repairs cover everything from a single slipped tile to a full ridge re-bedding. Because the fault types are so varied, prices swing more here than anywhere else on the roofline - a straightforward pointing repair might be £150 to £300, whereas a proper flashing rebuild around a chimney can climb past £900. The right first move is always a proper diagnosis, not a guess based on where the water shows up inside.
hubBody: The commonest calls are slipped or missing tiles (usually £120-£280 including access), cracked ridge tiles (often the sign of failed mortar bedding, £300-£800 for a full re-bed), and lead flashing pulling away around chimneys or party walls (£400-£1,100 depending on length). Newer builds increasingly have dry-fix ridge systems that don't need mortar at all - if yours is being re-bedded and it's post-2015, ask whether dry-fix is a like-for-like option.

Access adds a lot to a quote. A ladder-and-safety-rope job on a two-storey house doubles or triples once scaffolding or a tower is needed - which it usually is for anything past the first course of tiles. A reputable installer will always tell you upfront what the access approach is, and separate the material cost from the access cost so you can see what you're paying for.
hubTips: Insist on a photo of the fault before and after the repair - phone camera on a chimney access pole is fine, this is standard practice now.
For any work above the first course, ask whether scaffolding or a mobile tower is included - a ladder-only quote is a red flag for anything past minor slipped tiles.
Get the underlay checked while they're up there - torn or perished underfelt is often the real reason a leak keeps coming back after tile fixes.
Ask about the guarantee separately for the repair itself and for the surrounding tiles - some installers only guarantee what they touch.
roof-repair.commonSpecs: Slipped tile refixing with new clips, cracked ridge tile replacement, ridge re-bedding in fresh sand:cement 3:1 or dry-fix system, lead flashing renewal Code 4 or Code 5, chimney flaunching, verge repointing, underlay patch repair, ridge and hip mortar re-bed.

chimney-repair.hubIntro: Chimney work spans a huge range of jobs - from a £180 flaunching repair to a £3,000 full stack rebuild. The commonest calls are re-pointing eroded mortar, renewing the lead flashing where the stack meets the roof, replacing a cracked flaunching (the mortar bed at the top holding the pot in place), fitting a rain cap or bird guard, or a full rebuild when the brickwork above the roof line has failed. Chimney work is height access work - a decent quote always separates access cost from the actual repair.
hubBody: Diagnosis matters more here than anywhere else on the roof. A leak that shows up in the chimney breast can come from four different failure points: perished lead flashing (usually the culprit), cracked flaunching letting water into the stack, failed mortar joints on the brickwork above the roof, or a broken pot. A good installer will always send photos before quoting - insist on it, because 'the whole chimney needs rebuilding' quotes from someone who hasn't been up there yet are the classic upsell.

For a mid-range job (renew lead flashings + repoint the exposed brickwork + new flaunching + rain cap), expect £600-£1,200 including scaffold. A full rebuild above roof level is £1,500-£3,000 depending on stack height and access. Below that, a Code 4 lead flashing renewal alone is around £400-£700 and often solves the leak on its own. Anything involving the flue liner is a specialist HETAS job, not general roof work.
hubTips: Get photos of the fault before quoting - a scoped-out diagnosis beats a lump-sum 'rebuild it all' quote every time.
Ask what lead code the flashings will be replaced in - Code 4 is standard for domestic, Code 5 for exposed positions. Anything less is a corner cut.
Insist on scaffold or a tower for anything past a flaunching repair - a roof ladder job on a chimney is a fall risk and a corner-cutter's sign.
If the stack is disused, ask about a full removal to below roof level with a re-tile over - often cheaper than an ongoing repair cycle.
chimney-repair.commonSpecs: Code 4 or Code 5 lead flashing renewal (soakers, apron, back gutter, side flashings), lime or NHL 3.5 mortar repointing for pre-1919 property or S:C 1:3 for post-1919, new sand:cement flaunching, new pot bedding, C-cowl or bird guard rain cap, scaffold or aluminium tower access, HETAS specialist for any flue works.
